latin.701: GAR. Deinde opponitur, etiamsi lex illa permaneret, tamen abolitam esse respectu nostri, ut legales ceremonias, cum fuerit lex ceremonialis, cuius violatio non potest nobis imputari, quia non sumus sub ea lege; sicut violatio legum ceremonialium non potest nobis imputari, quia sub iis legibus non agimus. Resp. 1. Qui per Christum redempti sunt, & redemptionis illius participes, ii sane, ut a legibus ceremonialibus, ita etiam ab huius legis primitivae rigore liberati sunt, adeoque ad eos non spectant comminationes illi additae. Sed tamen, ut natura prior est gratiae (cum gratia naturae superveniat, eamque reformet & instaurat), & unusquisque concipitur prius esse homo, quam sit fidelis aut Christianus: Ita etiam status naturae, & lex sive foedus Naturale prius est foedere Gratiae, adeoque unusquisque consideratur prius sub foedere naturali, quam sub gratuito. Quare non debuit supponi, sed probari nos iam non esse sub ea lege.
latin.702: Nos vero contrario modo concludimus. Sumus naturaliter sub ea lege. Ergo eius violatio merito nobis imputatur. PLAC. Anne sumus naturaliter sub illa lege? Tenemur igitur eam observare.
latin.703: Imo Adamus quidem fuit sub illa lege. Non fuit enim naturaliter in paradiso, nec lex illa naturaliter lata est, sed supernaturaliter per verbum Dei. Sumus quidem sub lege naturae, quam & habitu, & actu, nimis, proh dolor, violamus. Sed quis non videt legem illam ceremonialem, & positivam, verbo Dei latam, liberi arbitrii libertatem circa rem natura sua moraliter nec bonam nec malam circumscribentem, hominique non quatenus homo fuit, aut mundi incola, sed tantum quatenus incola fuit paradisi, convenientem, non fuisse legem naturae? Putavitne Vir doctus nos naturaliter esse in paradiso terrestri? licere nobis vesci alijs arboribus paradisi?
latin.704: Ad legem autem naturae quod attinet, obligat omnes & singulos ad obedientiam, sed pro se quemque, & quamdiu est. Ostendi mihi velim aliquid in ea lege, unde probari possit primum primi hominis peccatum actuale omnibus illius posteris imputari debere immediate.
latin.705: GAR. Interim non est quod putemus legitimam esse illam argumentationem: legales ceremonias esse abrogatas; hanc esse legem ceremonialem; itaque abrogatam abolitamque. Nam legales ceremoniae, cum hic nominantur, sine dubitatione intelliguntur statuta illa ritualia sive ceremonalia, quae sunt a Deo Israeli constituta per manum Mosis; unde & ceremoniae Mosaicae vulgo dicuntur. Eas Christi adventu abrogatas fuisse nihil mirum est, cum umbrae essent & figurae quarum veritas & corpus est in Christo, Coloss. 2. 17. Respiciebant enim omnes ad Christum tanquam ad complementum suum. At ceremonia, quae in hac primitiva lege inerat, ad Christum non respiciebat tanquam ad significatum suum. Unde non consequitur, ut si ceremoniae illae Israeliticae antiquatae sunt, concludendum sit eo ipso, etiam abrogatam esse legem illam primordialem, ita ut nullus sit amplius eius usus, & ad homines nulla ratione spectet.
latin.706: PLAC. Misere me Viri docti tantum operae sumentis, ut probet legem de arbore scientiae boni & mali, quae nusquam alibi fuit quam in paradiso terrestri, & iam ab aliquot annorum millibus esse desiit in rerum natura, non esse antiquatam. Observat autem discrimen inter hanc primam legem ceremonialem, & Mosaicas ceremonias, quod nullum est, & ad confirmandum potius quam evertendum argumentum meum valere debet. Nam si ceremoniae legales erant typi adumbrantes ea quae Iesu Christi Evangelio revelata sunt, idem de ceremonia illa antiqua conficiendum est. Nonne enim & Adamus, & Eva, & paradisus terrestris, & arbor vitae, quae in eius erat medio, umbrae fuerunt quarum veritas & corpus est in Christo, aut saltem ad eius doctrinam pertinet? Quid est igitur, cur non idem sentiatur de arbore scientiae boni & mali?

pass_a.701: Garissoles meets the ceremonial-abrogate objection: even if the paradise ban remained, Placeus says it is abolished for us like legal ceremonies, since breach of a ceremonial law cannot be imputed when we are not under it. Reply: the redeemed are freed from that primal ban’s rigor as from ceremonial laws, so its threats do not look to them. Yet nature is prior to grace—grace comes upon nature and reforms and restores it—and each is first a human before a believer or Christian. So nature’s status and the natural law or covenant are prior to the covenant of grace; each is considered first under the natural covenant before the gracious. Therefore that we are already not under that law ought to have been proved, not merely supposed.
pass_a.702: Garissoles flips it: we are naturally under that law; therefore its breach is rightly imputed to us. Placeus asks: are we naturally under that law? Then we are bound to keep it.
pass_a.703: Placeus: Adam was under that law, but not by nature—he was not naturally in paradise, and the ban was given supernaturally by God’s word. We are under nature’s law, which habit and act we too much break. But who does not see that ceremonial positive ban—fencing free choice about a morally indifferent thing, fitting a man only as paradise’s dweller, not as man or world-dweller—was not nature’s law? Did the learned man think we are naturally in earthly paradise, free to eat its other trees?
pass_a.704: As for nature’s law: it binds all and each to obedience, but each for himself, and as long as he is. Let something in that law be shown from which Adam’s first actual sin must be immediately imputed to all his posterity.
pass_a.705: Garissoles: do not grant the chain that legal ceremonies are abrogated, that this ban was ceremonial, and therefore abrogated. When legal ceremonies are named here they mean without doubt the ritual statutes God set for Israel by Moses—commonly Mosaic ceremonies. That Christ’s coming abrogated them is no wonder: they were shadows and figures whose truth and body is in Christ (Col 2:17), all looking to him as their complement. But the ceremony inside this primitive law did not look to Christ as its significate. So it does not follow that antiquating those Israelite rites by that fact also abrogates the primordial law so that it has no further use and in no way looks to humans.
pass_a.706: Placeus pities the labor spent to prove the tree-of-knowledge ban—nowhere but in earthly paradise, gone from nature for millennia—is not antiquated. The alleged split between that first ceremonial law and Mosaic ceremonies is none, and should confirm rather than overturn his case. If legal ceremonies typed what the Gospel reveals, the same holds for that ancient ceremony. Were not Adam, Eve, earthly paradise, and the tree of life in its midst shadows whose truth and body are in Christ—or at least belong to his doctrine? Why not judge the tree of knowledge the same way?

701: GAR. Next it is opposed that even if that law remained, it has nonetheless been abolished with respect to us, as the legal ceremonies, since it was a ceremonial law, whose violation cannot be imputed to us because we are not under that law—just as violation of the ceremonial laws cannot be imputed to us because we do not live under those laws.

Reply 1. Those who have been redeemed through Christ, and are sharers in that redemption, have indeed been freed, as from the ceremonial laws, so also from the rigor of this primitive law, and so the threats added to it do not look to them.

But still, as nature is prior to grace (since grace comes upon nature and reforms and restores it), and each one is conceived to be a human before he is a believer or a Christian: so also the status of nature, and the law or Natural covenant, is prior to the covenant of Grace, and so each one is considered first under the natural covenant, before under the gracious.
Therefore it ought not to have been supposed, but proved, that we are already not under that law.
702: But we conclude in the contrary way.
We are naturally under that law.
Therefore its violation is deservedly imputed to us.
PLAC. Are we naturally under that law?
Then we are bound to observe it.
703: Yes—Adam indeed was under that law by nature? No: he was not naturally in paradise, nor was that law given naturally, but supernaturally through the word of God.
We are indeed under the law of nature, which both in habit and in act we too much, alas, violate.

But who does not see that that ceremonial and positive law, given by the word of God, fencing the freedom of free choice about a thing by its own nature morally neither good nor evil, and fitting a man not insofar as he was a human or an inhabitant of the world, but only insofar as he was an inhabitant of paradise, was not the law of nature?
Did the learned man think we are naturally in the earthly paradise? that it is lawful for us to eat of the other trees of paradise?
704: But as for the law of nature, it binds all and each to obedience—but each for himself, and as long as he is.
I would like something in that law to be shown me from which it can be proved that the first actual sin of the first man ought to be imputed immediately to all his posterity.
705: GAR. Meanwhile it is not to be thought that that argumentation is legitimate: that the legal ceremonies have been abrogated; that this is a ceremonial law; and so abrogated and abolished.

For legal ceremonies, when they are named here, are without doubt understood as those ritual or ceremonial statutes which God constituted for Israel by the hand of Moses; whence they are also commonly called Mosaic ceremonies.
That they were abrogated at Christ’s coming is no wonder, since they were shadows and figures whose truth and body is in Christ (Colossians 2:17).
For they all looked to Christ as to their complement.
But the ceremony which was in this primitive law did not look to Christ as to its significate.

Hence it does not follow that if those Israelite ceremonies have been antiquated, it must be concluded by that very fact that that primordial law has also been abrogated, so that there is no longer any use of it, and it in no way looks to humans.
706: PLAC. I pity the learned man taking so much pains to prove that the law about the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—which was nowhere else than in the earthly paradise, and for some thousands of years now has ceased to be in the nature of things—has not been antiquated.
But he observes a difference between this first ceremonial law and the Mosaic ceremonies which is none, and ought to avail to confirm rather than to overturn my argument.
For if the legal ceremonies were types shadowing the things revealed in the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the same is to be concluded about that ancient ceremony.
For were not Adam, and Eve, and the earthly paradise, and the tree of life which was in its midst, shadows whose truth and body is in Christ, or at least pertains to his doctrine?
What is there, then, why the same should not be held about the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?
